client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. There's this coffee shop she loved, and every time I walk past it or go inside, I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't seem to shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly — it feels like some things are just too heavy for words.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy, and I want you to know that the doubt you feel about whether words can even touch this kind of grief makes complete sense — sometimes loss feels bigger than language. I notice there's something very quiet and tender in the way you're speaking about her, almost like you're holding something fragile, even as the sadness feels so overwhelming. I'm curious — when you imagine sitting in that coffee shop she loved, what do you think she would have wanted you to feel there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I've thought about that question a lot, actually, and part of me wants to say she would have wanted me to feel peaceful or something like that, but honestly I don't know if I can trust that answer. It feels like I'm just making something up to make myself feel better, or worse, to make her into some kind of saint who had all these perfect wishes for me. The truth is I feel guilty even sitting there, like I don't deserve to be in a place she loved when I wasn't there for her the way I should have been at the end.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the feeling that you didn't show up the way you "should have" — is one of the most painful and common parts of grief, and it's worth gently asking: whose standard are you measuring yourself against when you say you weren't there enough? I also notice that even as you're speaking about something so raw, there's a kind of rushing quality to your words, like part of you is trying to get through this quickly — and I wonder if it feels safer to move fast past the guilt than to sit with it. What does "not being there the way I should have been" actually look like to you — what specifically are you holding yourself responsible for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess... when you ask it like that, whose standard, I don't really know. It's like there's this voice in my head that just says "you knew he was sick and you still didn't call more, you still let weeks go by," and I've never really questioned where that voice came from. And yeah, you're right that I was rushing — I think if I slow down I might actually start crying and I'm not sure I want to do that here.
therapist: There's something really courageous in what you just noticed — that the rushing might be a way of keeping the tears at bay — and I want you to know that crying here would be completely okay, even welcome, because it might be your grief asking for a little space. Your voice sounds very soft right now, almost like you're holding yourself very still on the inside even while the words are moving quickly, and I wonder if part of you is actually more ready to slow down than you think. That voice that says "you didn't call enough" — do you know if it sounds like anyone in particular, or is it purely your own?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hadn't thought about it sounding like anyone specific, but now that you ask... it does kind of sound like her, actually, like my mom's voice, which is strange because she was never really critical of me when she was alive. Maybe I've turned her into this judge in my head that she never actually was, and that feels like its own kind of loss, like I'm grieving a version of her that I distorted somehow. I don't know if I'm ready to cry, but something just got very tight in my chest when I said that.
therapist: What you just discovered feels really significant — that the critical voice might actually be a distortion of her, not her truth, and that recognizing that brings its own grief on top of grief. I notice that even as you said something so emotionally alive just now, your voice became very quiet and soft, almost like part of you was pulling inward while the words were reaching outward — as if something in you is absorbing this realization very privately, even while you're sharing it. Can you stay with that tightness in your chest for just a moment — not to force anything, but just to notice what it might be trying to tell you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'm staying with it... and honestly it feels like a kind of pressure, like something is being held together that doesn't want to be held together anymore. I think part of me has been so focused on managing the grief, on keeping it contained, that actually sitting with the idea that her voice got twisted inside me — that feels almost worse than the original loss somehow. Like I've been carrying a broken version of her this whole time and didn't know it.
therapist: What you just said — that carrying a broken version of her feels almost worse than the loss itself — strikes me as one of the most honest and tender things you've shared, and I want to reflect back that this isn't a failure on your part, it's what grief does when we love someone and don't have enough space to process the loss slowly. I notice your voice has become very soft and quick, like the words are coming from somewhere deep and a little fragile, and that makes sense given how much you're holding right now. I'm wondering — now that you can see this distorted version of her for what it is, what do you think the *real* her, the one who was never actually critical, might want to say to you in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I want to say she'd tell me it's okay, that she loved me and wasn't disappointed in me... but honestly, I don't fully trust that answer right now. It feels like I'm just making up what I want to hear, and I'm scared that if I put words in her mouth, I'm distorting her even more. I guess I'm worried that anything I imagine her saying is just me trying to comfort myself, and that feels kind of hollow.
therapist: The fear of "making things up" is actually a sign of how much integrity you're bringing to this — you don't want to dishonor her by putting false words in her mouth, and that itself is a form of love. But I want to gently offer this: you spent years knowing her, absorbing who she was, and the part of you that believes she loved you without disappointment isn't invention — it's memory, it's evidence. What would it feel like to treat that sense of her love not as something you're making up, but as something you actually earned the right to know?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That's... a really different way to think about it, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But I keep coming back to this fear that I'm just telling myself what I want to hear, you know, that I'm constructing a version of her that makes me feel less guilty about the distance that was there in the last few years. Like, what if the love I'm remembering is real but I'm conveniently leaving out the parts where I let her down?
therapist: What strikes me is that you're not actually trying to erase the hard parts — the fact that you keep pulling them back in, that you won't let yourself off the hook too easily, suggests you're genuinely trying to hold the whole truth of the relationship, not just the comfortable version. In CBT we'd call what you're doing "all-or-nothing thinking" in reverse — instead of idealizing her, you're afraid that any comfort you feel must mean you're hiding something, as if love and disappointment can't coexist in the same honest memory. I'm curious — is it possible that she both loved you fully *and* that there were moments you fell short, and that neither of those things cancels the other out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true — that both things can exist at once without one canceling the other out. But when I actually try to sit with that, it feels almost too convenient, like I'm just giving myself permission to feel okay when maybe I don't deserve to. It's like if I accept the comfort, I'm somehow betraying her by not holding myself fully accountable for the ways I let her down.
therapist: There's something I want to name gently — your words are saying "maybe I can almost believe this," but your voice sounds much more distressed than that, like something underneath is pulling quite hard against the idea of letting yourself off the hook at all. I wonder if "holding yourself accountable" has quietly become a way of staying close to her — like as long as you're punishing yourself, you're still in relationship with the loss, and accepting comfort might feel like letting go of her altogether. Does that resonate at all, or does it feel wide of the mark?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually hit me harder than I expected, and I'm not sure what to do with that. Like, there's something in what you said that feels uncomfortably true — that if I stop blaming myself for my mom's death, it might mean I'm just... moving on without her. But I also don't know if I can trust that feeling, because it sounds almost too neat, too psychological, like maybe I'm just agreeing because it sounds right and not because it actually is.
therapist: The way you just said that — your voice carrying something much more raw and strained than your words are quite letting on — makes me think part of you already knows this is true, even while your mind is working hard to find reasons to doubt it. And I want to honor that skepticism, because it's protective and it's yours, but I also notice you said "my mom's death" just now — not her passing, not losing her — and I wonder if that word choice is telling us something about the weight you've been quietly carrying. What would it mean for you, in the most concrete and personal sense, if staying in the grief really has been a way of staying close to her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hadn't really noticed that I said "death" instead of something softer, but now that you're pointing it out, it feels like it matters somehow, like I was being more honest than I meant to be. And your question... it kind of stops me cold, because if staying in the grief is how I stay close to her, then getting better would feel like abandoning her. That's terrifying to even say out loud, because it makes me sound like I'm choosing to suffer, and I don't want to believe that about myself.
therapist: What you just said out loud — that getting better might feel like abandoning her — took real courage, and I want you to sit with the fact that you said it, because naming something that terrifying is not the same as choosing it. You're not choosing to suffer; you learned, somewhere in the grief, that suffering was the only language left that kept you connected to her, and that's not a character flaw — it's a testament to how much she mattered. I'm wondering, slowly and gently — is there any part of you that can imagine staying deeply connected to who she really was, the loving and non-judgmental her, without the suffering being the price of admission?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
